The inserted nine-word relative clause identifies those people by the liturgical action just completed: devout remembrance of the Son's Passion and death. It adds no new requested gift, image, comparison or independent petition. The reordered supplication and the received same-Christ conclusion/response are conventional liturgical framing. On that bounded view, the whole can be proposed as a functional contextual adaptation of the single old blessing, rather than a newly selected collection of old fragments. This is an arguable finite qualified-nonoriginal-adaptation assessment at moderate confidence, not proof of an exact ancient whole or an adopted publication conclusion. The full relative clause and the new placement must still be judged as part of the resulting whole. Strongest contrary: The newly inserted full relative clause gives a specific commemorative rationale and ties the old blessing to the Good Friday assembly. Even where its vocabulary is conventional, this substantive clause and the resulting whole-prayer arrangement cannot be classed as mere spelling, inflection or punctuation. No exact premodern witness for that entire target clause in this whole has been established. The antiquity of the five petitions and the conventional conclusion do not alone settle originality of the modern whole. prior_negative_finding.evidence: WHAT I CHECKED. (1) I read the 1862's own end of the Good Friday liturgy, text-layer lines 33352-33460, printed pp. 178-179. After the priest's communion it prints `Quod ore sumpsimus, Domine...` and then, in terms, `Non dicitur Corpus tuum, Domine, nec Postcommunio, nec Placeat tibi, nec datur benedictio: sed, facta reverentia Altari, Sacerdos cum ministris discedit`. The pre-1955 rite has NO prayers after Communion on this day; the 1955 Ordo added three, because it restored the Communion of the people. (2) I then searched the whole 1862 by incipit and by four distinctive phrases -- `Super p.pulum tuum`, `benedicti. copi.sa`, `indulg.ntia veniat`, `succr.scat`, `devota mente` -- over the flattened, dehyphenated stream. `Super populum` occurs many times as the Lenten rubric `Oratio super populum` and once as `benedictio copiosa descendat: quae et sanctificationem nobis clementer...`, which is a DIFFERENT Lenten super populum prayer, not this one. `devota mente` and `succrescat` occur nowhere in the book. SAME CANDOUR AS FOR no. 924: the prayer is very likely ancient, but no tracked public-domain witness carries it, so it may not be published from this facsimile on the evidence available here. || THREE-BOOK SWEEP ADDED IN THE SECOND PASS. The lane's first pass swept the 1862 alone. On the coordinator's rule that new-matter needs the whole shelf behind it, I re-swept all three tracked public-domain witnesses -- 1862 Pustet (108,905 lines), 1604 Vatican typica (63,205 lines), 1570 Venice (84,443 lines), the last two with long s folded to s -- on rare word PAIRS taken adjacent in the 1962 text and matched fuzzily (>=0.85 character similarity, same initial letter) within a twelve-word window, so neither a lost ornamental capital nor a damaged accent can hide a hit. POSITIVE CONTROL for the procedure: it fires on prayers this lane proved present (oblationibus+hostiarum 3 hits in the 1862, hostiarum+initiata 2, productum+silice 1, paschalia+inflammari 1, illustras+conserva 1, segetum+spinarum 1). RESULT: zero in all three books on succrescat+firmetur, firmetur+eundem, devota+recoluit, recoluit+copiosa, copiosa+indulgentia, tribuatur+succrescat, succrescat+redemptio, redemptio+firmetur. Single token succrescat occurs nowhere in any of the three. The two isolated ones (indulgentia+consolatio in the 1862, recoluit+descendat in the 1862 and 1570) are common-word coincidences, opened and not this prayer.

latin_provenance.publication_evidence: Consider the resulting prayer as one adapted collect: its complete inherited movement remains divine restoration through Christ's Passion, a request to preserve mercy's work within the speakers, and the purpose of living in perpetual devotion in relation to the mystery. The modern wording makes death explicit, casts restoration as accomplished, names the mercy already central to the old petition, uses a collective singular work, and connects the petition to participation after Communion. The changes adjust the old collect to its specific liturgical use without adding a new requested benefit, metaphor, narrative or separate source-selected petition. With the independently witnessed conventional same-Christ conclusion and response, that whole is a viable finite qualified-nonoriginal-adaptation proposal at moderate confidence. This is an inference about the measured adaptation, not a grant based on familiar words or the old prayer's age. The cumulative changes in address, tense, number and celebration/participation still require a whole-expression decision. Strongest contrary: The accumulated changes recast the divine address, explicitly add death, shift the restoration from present to completed action, change plural works to one work, and replace celebration with participation in the mystery. These coordinated theological and rhetorical choices must be considered together. Conventional vocabulary and a recognizable old prayer skeleton do not prove that the whole modern arrangement is unprotected. No exact premodern whole target witness has been established.
